row.final_message:
The tests pass: 4 passed, exit code 0. That includes the new test, which checks that "Café Olé" gives "cafe-ole" and "Über Señor" gives "uber-senor". The three original tests also still pass, so "Hello, World!", the whitespace handling, the length cap and post_url behave as before.

What the run doesn't show:
- It covers only the examples in the test file. I haven't checked other accented inputs, and I haven't diffed the old and new output over a set of existing titles. The "ASCII slugs stay exactly as they are" claim rests on reading the code, since NFD only affects non-ASCII characters. If you have a list of real post titles, comparing old and new slugs would be a better check.
- Letters with no accent decomposition (ß, ø, æ, ł, Cyrillic, Greek, CJK) are still dropped, so your "every character from any language" request is not done. The open question is recorded, and it needs a decision between a transliteration dependency like unidecode, a hand-written mapping, or Unicode slugs.
- One thing to flag for Jonas: this changes existing URLs for any past post whose title had accents, for example "caf-ol" becomes "cafe-ole". Those posts will need redirects, or their old links will break.

I can't open the pull request because I have no tool for it, and I couldn't put the test result on the claim ledger because no record_claim tool is available here. The changed files are slugs.py and tests/test_slugs.py. To open the PR, commit those two files, push the branch, and open it for Jonas. Mention the URL change and the unresolved non-Latin question in the description.

 import re

cli.stdout:
From the files I read: slugify lowercases the title and then replaces everything outside a-z0-9 with a hyphen. The docstring already says "Café" -> "cafe", but nothing in the code does that, so é is simply dropped.

Proposed fix: normalize to NFD (which splits é into e plus a combining accent) and remove the combining marks before the existing regex. I'm using NFD instead of NFKD so only accents change. Everything else, including whitespace, hyphens, max_len and the ASCII-only output, behaves as it does now. I'll also add a regression test. Both writes need your approval. After that I'd like to run the tests.

I'm not doing the "every character from any language" part. NFD only fixes letters that are a base letter plus an accent (é, ü, ñ). Letters like ß, ø, æ, ł, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK have no such decomposition, so they will still be dropped. Handling them means either a hand-written mapping, which is always incomplete, or a transliteration dependency such as `unidecode`. Cyrillic or CJK titles would then get romanized slugs that may read poorly. The other option is to allow Unicode in URLs, which breaks your "ASCII slugs stay as they are" constraint. I've noted this as an open question so you and Jonas can decide.
